model.modifications: Procedural 3D leaf anatomy tissue cross-section exported as GLB.

short.en: A thin waterproof waxy coating on top of the leaf that stops excess water loss.

detail.en: Extracellular hydrophobic layer made of cutin secreted by epidermal cells. Allows sunlight to pass through while sharply reducing uncontrolled cuticular transpiration.

short.en: A single transparent protective layer of tightly packed cells on the leaf's top surface.

detail.en: Usually lacks chloroplasts (except guard cells) and stomata in most dicot leaves, letting light penetrate directly to the palisade layer beneath.

short.en: Tall, tightly packed green cells packed with chloroplasts — the main site of photosynthesis.

detail.en: Elongated columnar parenchyma cells arranged vertically beneath the upper epidermis. Rich in chloroplasts aligned along cell edges to maximise light absorption.

short.en: Loosely arranged green cells with gaps around them so gases can move easily.

detail.en: Rounded/irregular chlorenchyma cells below the palisade layer with large intercellular air spaces connecting directly to the stomata for CO₂ and O₂ diffusion.

short.en: Tubular vessels inside the leaf vein that bring water and minerals from the roots.

detail.en: Located on the adaxial (upper) side of the vascular bundle in a leaf. Dead, lignified tracheids and vessels conduct water upward by transpiration pull.

short.en: Living tubes inside the leaf vein that carry made food (sugars) to the rest of the plant.

detail.en: Located on the abaxial (lower) side of the vascular bundle. Sieve tube elements and companion cells translocate sucrose bidirectionally via pressure-flow.

short.en: The protective bottom layer of the leaf, containing tiny openings called stomata.

detail.en: Bears most stomata in dorsiventral (dicot) leaves so gas exchange occurs on the cooler, shaded underside, reducing water evaporation.

short.en: Tiny adjustable pores on the underside of the leaf for breathing (CO₂ in, O₂ & water vapour out).

detail.en: Each stoma is flanked by two kidney-shaped (dicot) or dumbbell-shaped (monocot) guard cells containing chloroplasts. Guard cells swell with K⁺ and water to open the pore in daylight.

short.en: Protective ring of parenchyma cells wrapping around the leaf's xylem and phloem.

detail.en: In C₄ plants (like maize and sugarcane), thick-walled bundle sheath cells form a wreath ('Kranz anatomy') around vascular bundles where RuBisCO performs the Calvin cycle.

short.en: Open gas pockets in the spongy layer allowing rapid CO₂ diffusion to cells.

detail.en: Substomatal cavities and intercellular air channels form a continuous gas phase inside the leaf so CO₂ entering via stomata reaches mesophyll surfaces quickly.

question.en: Tap the tall, tightly packed green cells where most photosynthesis takes place.

explanation.en: Palisade mesophyll cells sit right under the clear upper epidermis and are packed with chloroplasts to capture maximum sunlight.

question.en: What is the main job of the stomata and guard cells?

options.en: Anchor the leaf to the stem
Let CO₂ in and O₂ / water vapour out
Carry sugars from roots to leaves

explanation.en: Stomata open and close using guard cells to allow carbon dioxide into the leaf for photosynthesis and release oxygen and water vapour.

question.en: Tap the tubes in the leaf vein that bring water from the roots.

explanation.en: Xylem sits on the upper side of the leaf vein and delivers water and dissolved minerals from the roots.

question.en: In C₄ plants exhibiting Kranz anatomy, which structure forms a concentric ring around the vascular bundle?

explanation.en: Large, agranal-chloroplast-rich bundle sheath cells surround the vascular bundles in Kranz anatomy to concentrate CO₂ around RuBisCO and minimise photorespiration.
